questions.q: Why does acknowledging an incident immediately matter, even before the cause is known?
options: Silence in the first hour reads as denial or indifference, even if the team is actively investigating
Acknowledging immediately is legally required in every jurisdiction
It has no effect on user trust either way
It allows the team to skip writing a postmortem later
questions.explain: Users watching a protocol's channels interpret silence negatively; a prompt acknowledgment signals the team is aware and working the problem.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend stating only confirmed facts in early communication, rather than speculating about cause or scope?
options: A wrong early guess has to be walked back later, which costs more trust than waiting for confirmation would have
Speculating early is always more accurate than waiting for facts
Teams are never allowed to update their statements once published
Confirmed facts are never available until a postmortem is fully published
questions.explain: An incorrect early claim about cause or scope damages credibility when it has to be corrected -- waiting for confirmation avoids that cost.

questions.q: What does the 'timeline' section of a postmortem draw directly from, according to this lesson?
options: Lesson 24's alert history and monitoring data -- what happened, in order, with timestamps
A press release drafted by the marketing team
Guesses made after the incident is already resolved
The original smart contract's test suite from Chapter 1
questions.explain: The alert history kept during incident response becomes the raw material for reconstructing an accurate, timestamped timeline.

questions.q: What does 'root cause' mean in the context of a real postmortem, as described in this lesson?
options: The actual technical mechanism behind the failure, and why existing tests or reviews didn't catch it -- not just "a bug was found"
A vague reference to "a bug" with no further technical detail required
The name of the individual engineer responsible for the error
A summary of the protocol's total value locked at the time of the incident
questions.explain: A useful root cause explanation names the actual mechanism and explains why prior safeguards (tests, reviews, CI) didn't catch it.

questions.q: What does 'blameless, not toothless' mean for a postmortem process?
options: The process focuses on systemic causes rather than individual fault, but every remediation item still needs a named owner and a due date
No changes are ever made as a result of a postmortem
Individual engineers must be publicly named and blamed for every incident
Remediation items are optional and never need to be assigned to anyone
questions.explain: Blameless focuses on what let the incident happen at a systemic level; toothless would mean no one is accountable for actually fixing it -- this lesson rejects that.
